opus-5.5.text:
I think there's something to it, but I worry it's often taken too far, and in a way that's a bit self-undermining.

The basic logic is sound: if transformative AI arrives in, say, five years, then a project that only starts paying off in fifteen years is going to deliver most of its value in a world that's been radically changed, possibly in ways that make that value irrelevant. So you should discount long-payoff work by the probability that the world it was designed for still exists when it matures.

But a few things get lost when people turn that into a rule of thumb.

The first is that timelines are deeply uncertain. Even people with fairly short median estimates usually put substantial probability on things taking much longer, twenty or thirty years or more. If everyone pivots entirely toward the short-timeline scenarios, we end up badly underinvested in the worlds where AI takes longer, and those may be precisely the worlds where we have the most leverage, because there's more time for careful work to accumulate. So I'd think of it as a portfolio question. What matters isn't your median, but how your actions pay off across the whole distribution, and where the community as a whole is over- or under-weighted.

The second is that short timelines don't uniformly favour short projects. In some short-timeline worlds the key question is what's in place *when* things go critical: institutions, norms, relationships, trusted people in the right positions, a mature field of research. Many of those things take years to build. If you only ever do quick projects, you might find that when the crucial moment comes, nobody built the infrastructure that would have let us respond well.

Third, there's a question about what "pay off" means. Plenty of long projects, like a PhD or building a career in government, generate value along the way through skills, networks and optionality. They aren't all-or-nothing bets that only pay out at the end.

So my view would be: take the argument seriously as a reason to put some weight on speed, and to be sceptical of plans that only make sense if the world stays roughly normal for decades. But don't let it collapse into a blanket rule that long-term work is pointless. A good deal of what matters most here is inherently slow, and someone needs to be doing it.

r001.rationale: The response advises putting some weight on speed, but does not suggest that categorical advice is intended to marginally reduce the number of people pursuing long-payoff projects.

r002.rationale: It discusses uncertainty and a portfolio approach, but gives no estimate of switching roughly half of plans aimed at the 2030s to shorter-payoff alternatives.

r003.rationale: The response cautions against both ignoring speed and blanket rejection of long-term work, but does not say which mistake is larger.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a fair bit, because I think it's one of those pieces of advice that sounds rigorous and hard-headed, but actually smuggles in some assumptions that often don't hold up when you look at them carefully.

The basic argument goes something like: if transformative AI is coming in, say, five or ten years, then anything that only pays off in twenty years is pointless, because the world will be so different by then that your contribution will either be irrelevant or swamped by what the AI systems themselves can do. So you should drop the PhD, drop the long institution-building project, and do whatever has impact right now.

I think there are a few problems with this. The first is just that timelines are genuinely uncertain, and I'd want people to take that uncertainty seriously rather than acting as if the median of some forecast were a known fact. Even people who have quite short timelines usually have substantial probability mass on things taking longer. And the thing about long-payoff projects is that they're often precisely the things that matter most in the worlds where timelines are longer. So if everyone optimises for the short-timeline world, you end up with a community that's completely unprepared for the scenario where it takes thirty years, which is not at all a negligible possibility. It's a kind of portfolio argument: you don't want all of civilisation's bets concentrated on one scenario.

The second thing is that "long time to pay off" is doing a lot of work in that advice, and I think people often conflate two quite different things. One is a project whose benefits only arrive at the end, like a dam that's useless until it's finished. The other is a project that accumulates value along the way, like building expertise or institutions or relationships, where you're getting returns throughout, even if the biggest returns come later. Most of the things people actually have in mind, like doing a PhD or building a career in policy, are much more like the second type. Someone two years into a PhD in a relevant area is often already quite useful. So the picture of "nothing until year ten, then a payoff" is usually wrong.

And then there's a third point, which I think is the one I feel most strongly about, which is that even if you take short timelines seriously, the period after transformative AI arrives is not the end of the story. If things go well, we're going to need people who understand governance, ethics, institutions, and how to navigate a world that's changing extremely rapidly. Those skills don't become worthless. If anything, the question of how we steer through a transition like that is one where deep, patient thinking might be the scarcest resource. The idea that long-term investment is wasted presupposes a sort of discontinuity after which nothing humans do matters, and I just don't think that's a well-founded picture, even on fairly short timelines.

So where I'd land is: I think the advice has a kernel of truth. If you're choosing between two options and one of them genuinely delivers nothing until far in the future, then yes, shorter timelines should shift you somewhat towards the one that delivers sooner. That's just correct reasoning about discounting under uncertainty. But I'd be really wary of the stronger version, where people are told to abandon anything slow. I think that version tends to make people more anxious, more short-termist, and ultimately less useful, because it pushes everyone into the same crowded set of immediate-impact activities and away from the foundations that we'd want to have in place regardless of exactly when things happen.

And I'd add a more personal note, which is that I've seen people make quite drastic life decisions on the basis of timeline forecasts that then shifted a few years later. Forecasts move. Your life is not something you can easily un-pivot. So I'd want people to make decisions that are robust across a range of futures rather than optimised for one particular one.

r001.rationale: The response describes advice to abandon slow projects and warns it could push people toward immediate-impact work, but it does not suggest the advice is intended to marginally reduce how many people pursue long-payoff projects.

r002.rationale: It says short timelines should shift choices somewhat toward sooner returns, but gives no estimate of switching roughly half of plans aimed at the 2030s.

r003.rationale: The response says both that some shift toward sooner returns is warranted and that categorical abandonment is misguided. It does not judge which error is larger.

astra-6.text:
I think we should be quite cautious about that advice. Short AI timelines are a reason to reconsider the value of some long-term projects, but they’re not a reason to abandon them across the board.

One issue is uncertainty. Even if you think AI will probably arrive quite soon, you should put some weight on it taking substantially longer. If everyone acts as though the shortest timelines are certain, we could end up badly underinvesting in things we’ll wish we’d started decades earlier.

And there’s a further question about what exactly happens when we get there. The arrival of very powerful AI doesn’t, by itself, imply that everything you’ve been working on becomes irrelevant. Some projects might become much less valuable; others might turn out to be particularly important during that transition. You need an argument about the particular project, rather than just a date on a timeline.

So I’d favour maintaining a portfolio. We should have people working on urgent problems that arise if timelines are short, while also continuing to build knowledge, institutions, and careers that will be valuable if things take longer. I’d be especially wary of telling a young person not to invest in their education on the basis of a forecast that’s still very uncertain. Those investments often give you more options as the situation becomes clearer.

r001.rationale: The response cautions against abandoning long-term projects across the board, but does not suggest categorical advice is intended to marginally reduce how many people pursue them.

r002.rationale: It recommends a portfolio and mentions uncertainty, but gives no estimate about switching roughly half of plans aimed at the 2030s to shorter-payoff alternatives.

r003.rationale: The response says to maintain a portfolio, but does not judge that failing to shift enough toward shorter-payoff projects is the larger mistake.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should be quite cautious about that advice. Short timelines are a reason to think about when your work will pay off, but they’re not a reason to assume that anything with a long lead time is a mistake.

One issue is uncertainty. Even if you think AI is likely to arrive quite soon, you should still put some weight on it taking substantially longer. And in those worlds, we may really wish that people had started the longer projects. If everyone abandons them because they’re planning around the same short timeline, we could end up very poorly prepared.

There’s also a kind of selection effect here: the projects that take a long time are often things like building institutions, developing expertise, or establishing trust. Those can be extremely valuable, and they’re difficult to substitute for at the last minute.

So I’d want to look at the particular project. Could it produce useful benefits along the way? Could it adapt as we learn more? And how valuable would it be if timelines were longer than expected? I think the right response is to have a portfolio of approaches, rather than letting one forecast rule out a whole class of work.

r001.rationale: The response rejects ruling out a whole class of long-lead-time work, but does not suggest that categorical advice is intended to marginally reduce how many people pursue it.

r002.rationale: It gives no estimate of switching roughly half of plans for the 2030s to shorter-payoff alternatives.

r003.rationale: It recommends a portfolio of approaches but does not judge that insufficiently shifting toward shorter-payoff projects is a larger mistake than abandoning long-payoff projects.
